cards.heading: Why QoS
cards.body: When a link is congested, QoS decides which traffic waits and which is dropped. Voice and video need low delay, jitter and loss: voice wants under 150 ms one way, under 30 ms jitter and under 1% loss.

cards.heading: Classification and marking
cards.body: Traffic is classified (by ACL, NBAR application recognition, or incoming markings) and marked as close to the source as possible. Layer 2: 802.1Q CoS (3 bits, 0-7). Layer 3: the DSCP field (6 bits, 0-63) in the IP header's ToS byte. CoS is the 3-bit 802.1p priority in the 802.1Q tag (values 0-7). DSCP is 6 bits of the IPv4 ToS / IPv6 Traffic Class byte; the other 2 bits are ECN.
cards.example:
EF 46        voice
AF41 34      video
AF21-23      business data
CS0 / 0      best effort
CS6 48       network control
cards.mnemonic:
EF 46 is voice: Expedited Forwarding, because a phone call can't wait. Only network control (CS6 48, CS7 56) sits above it.
AF classes follow a formula, AFxy = 8x + 2y, so AF41 = 32 + 2 = 34. CS values are 8 × the class, so CS6 = 48.
Easy to mix up: in AFxy a higher x is more important, but a higher y is dropped first.
CoS has 3 bits (0-7) and DSCP has 6 bits (0-63): DSCP has twice the bits.

cards.heading: AF arithmetic
cards.body: Assured Forwarding AFxy: x is the class (1-4, higher is better treatment), y the drop probability (1-3, higher is dropped first). DSCP = 8x + 2y.

cards.heading: Trust boundary
cards.body: Devices only honour markings they trust. Typically the access switch trusts an IP phone's markings but re-marks traffic from PCs. The trust boundary is where markings start being believed. With Cisco IP phones on the access ports, the boundary is at the phone and access switch port: the switch trusts the phone's markings (often only when CDP detects a phone) and re-marks the PC's.

cards.heading: Queuing
cards.body: Packets wait in queues during congestion. CBWFQ gives each class a guaranteed share of bandwidth; LLQ adds a strict-priority queue for voice, policed so it can't starve the others. Without QoS there's one FIFO queue.

cards.heading: Congestion avoidance
cards.body: A full queue tail-drops everything new, which makes many TCP flows back off together and then surge (global synchronisation). WRED drops some packets early, more for higher drop-probability markings, so TCP flows slow down gradually.

cards.heading: Policing and shaping
cards.body: Both enforce a rate. Policing drops (or re-marks) excess traffic immediately, often inbound at an ISP edge. Shaping buffers the excess and sends it later, smoothing the rate at the cost of delay; it's used outbound towards a slower provider rate.
